Marine Board's Opportunities and Access Report incorporates information from federal and state agencies, local facility operators and fellow boaters to provide up-to-date information so boaters can decide where to recreate and what to expect this season. Subscribe to receive email updates.

Updates by waterbody

ALDRICH PONDS (Roosevelt and Stewart Lakes): Trout (2 fish limit)

Access to the ponds is now open and both ponds have been stocked for 2026. There are some excellent quality holdover fish in both ponds with recent reports suggesting fishing is good.

GRANDE RONDE RIVER: Trout, whitefish, smallmouth bass, steelhead

Flows on the Grande Ronde River have dropped to summertime base levels. Trout fishing will likely slow during this time of year when water temperatures are elevated. However, bass can be caught using a variety of techniques.

Fishing for steelhead opened on September 1, however, most steelhead bound for the Grande Ronde River are still making their way up the Columbia and Snake Rivers. Steelhead fishing will probably be slow until more fish arrive later into October. Last updated 9/3/26.

Links to the following river gauges:

Grande Ronde River Below Clear Creek, Near Starkey

Grande Ronde River, Near Perry

Grande Ronde River at Troy

HAT ROCK POND: Trout

Anglers should find success throughout the summer using PowerBait, worms or spinners, and focus their efforts in the mornings or evenings. Last updated 8/24/26.

IMNAHA RIVER: Trout, whitefish, bass

Fishing for trout and whitefish can be good throughout the middle and upper Imnaha River. Trout can be caught on a variety of flies and lures. Anglers targeting whitefish should drift weighted nymphs through deeper holes. Bass can be caught by anglers in the lower portion of the river, especially downstream of Cow Creek. Note that angling for salmon is prohibited throughout the Imnaha River including catch and release.

Fishing for steelhead opened on September 1, however, most steelhead bound for the Imnaha River are still making their way up the Columbia and Snake Rivers. Steelhead fishing will probably be slow until more fish arrive later into October. Last updated 9/3/26.

JOHN DAY RIVER: Bass, trout

Due to multiple large wildfires in the John Day Basin, access to the river is closed in many areas. The Prineville BLM has closed access to several areas within the John Day Basin, including some boat launches. The Twickenham boat launch, which is managed by ODFW on private lands, is also closed in addition to several boat launches on BLM lands in the vicinity of Mitchell and Clarno. Be sure to consult the Prineville BLM webpage for current closure information. Current river flows are extremely low. Last updated 8/17/26.

JUBILEE LAKE: Rainbow trout

Access to Jubilee Lake is currently open and fishing should be good. Last updated 8/31/26.

LOOKINGGLASS CREEK: Rainbow trout, mountain whitefish

Fishing for Chinook Salmon closed on June 14. Regulations for fishing Lookingglass Creek reverted to permanent regulations available in the 2026 regulation booklet. Throughout the summer, trout and whitefish will be available to anglers fishing at Lookingglass Creek. No new reports. Last updated 7/22/26.

MAGONE LAKE: Rainbow and brook trout

Fishing is often good year-round, and the lake has been stocked for 2026.

McNARY PONDS: Walleye, bass and trout

Trout will likely be most active in the morning and late evening hours. Bass fishing can also be good during the summer months. Last updated 8/17/26.

McKAY RESERVOIR: Bass, perch, rainbow trout

Be advised that McKay Reservoir is currently being used as a source of water for fire suppression. Refuge gates are currently locked and boating is prohibited. Bank angling is still allowed. Fishing for bass and panfish has been good on McKay Reservoir. The Oregon Health Authority has issued a precaution for harmful algae blooms. The reservoir is currently 31% full. Last updated 8/24/26.

MORGAN LAKE: Largemouth bass, rainbow trout

Access to Morgan Lake is now again open. Please see the City of La Grande's website for more information. Largemouth bass and trout are available for anglers until October 31 when fishing regularly closes at Morgan Lake. Last updated 9/7/26.

PENLAND LAKE: Rainbow trout

Fishing for rainbow trout is currently very good on Penland Lake. Shore anglers have been having good success near the boat launch with power bait. Last updated 8/24/26.

UMATILLA RIVER: Fall Chinook, coho, summer steelhead, trout, bass, walleye

Fishing for salmon and steelhead opens on September 1. Expect catch rates to increase as we get closer to October. There is now a new regulation in place with a hook gap size that may not exceed 3/8 inch in the section of the Umatilla River above the CTUIR reservation. This new regulation is to protect bull trout and decrease the chance of hooking mortality. As a reminder, if you catch a bull trout, recognized by its white spots, please keep it in the water and release it as quickly as possible. Targeting bull trout is NOT allowed in the Umatilla River. Last updated 8/24/26.

WALLOWA COUNTY PONDS: Rainbow trout

Local ponds including Victor, Weaver, and Marr Pond have been stocked with rainbow trout. These ponds should provide good fishing throughout the summer along with various forest ponds that have also been stocked. Anglers can be successful using a variety of lures, flies, and baits. Kinney Lake has drained. It will be restocked after it begins to fill again later into fall. Last updated 8/17/26.

WALLOWA LAKE: Rainbow trout, kokanee, lake trout

Wallowa Lake has been stocked with rainbow trout that readily take lures, flies, and dough baits. Fishing for trout will be best near shore especially on the South end of the lake near the inlet of the Wallowa River. Anglers are still catching some very nice kokanee. Most kokanee are now at depths > 45 feet. Both trolling and jigging can be effective ways of catching kokanee during this time of year. Using a fish finder and a downrigger can help anglers find the depths where kokanee are holding and present lures to them.

Kokanee have started spawning in the Wallowa River above the lake. They can readily be seen throughout Wallowa Lake State Park and make for some great fall wildlife viewing. Last updated 9/7/26.

WALLOWA RIVER: Whitefish, trout

Trout and whitefish can be caught on a variety of baits, lures, and flies. Casting flies like wooly buggers and nymphs to pockets of slower moving water near shore can be good ways to catch fish on the Wallowa River. Fishing dry flies or nymphs under a bobber can be very productive. Recently, flows have dropped and fishing may be slower, especially on warmer days. Note that due to low water and warm temperatures extra care should be taken when handling fish. Follow best catch and release ethics to give the fish the best chance at survival and consider giving fish a break in late afternoon. No new reports. Last updated 7/27/26.

WILLOW CREEK RESERVOIR: Trout, crappie, bass

Recent sampling on Willow Creek Reservoir resulted in a good number of nice sized largemouth bass being collected. Anglers have been catching some nice trout from the shore near the boat launch as well as bass and crappie from boats. As a reminder, there is a 25 fish limit for crappie on Willow Creek Reservoir.

This spring, district staff installed 12 artificial habitat structures bringing the total number of structures on the reservoir to 22. These structures were put in place to provide fish habitat when the reservoir is drawn down.

The Oregon Health Authority has issued a precaution for harmful algae blooms. Follow this link to see the Oregon Health Authorities website showing harmful algae bloom advisories. Last updated 8/24/26.

Columbia Fishing

September 10, 2026

Current and upcoming fishing opportunities:

Columbia River fall salmon seasons opened August 1, see the regulation update page for details.

Announcements

For the latest regulations, including in-season changes see the fishing regulation update page.

Forecasts for 2026 Columbia River Spring Chinook, Summer Chinook, Fall Chinook, Coho, and Sockeye are available here.

Fish consumption advisories

The Oregon Health Authority has issued consumption guidelines for parts of the Columbia River due to high levels of mercury and/or PCBs. Fish with these chemicals look, act, smell and taste like any other fish, so caution is important.

SALMON, STEELHEAD, AND SHAD

On Saturday's (9/5) flight, there were 828 boats and 24 bank anglers from Bonneville Dam to Warrior Rock.

Gorge: Weekly checking showed 158 Chinook, 31 jack Chinook, and one coho kept, and 24 Chinook, two jack Chinook, and one coho released for 82 boats (253 anglers); and five Chinook and two jack Chinook kept for 33 bank anglers.

Troutdale: Weekly checking showed 123 Chinook, 13 jack Chinook, and one coho kept, and 13 Chinook, one Chinook jack, and four coho released for 228 boats (472 anglers).

PDX to Warrior Rock Lighthouse: Weekly checking showed 649 Chinook, 81 jack Chinook, and 41 coho kept, and 88 Chinook, 34 jack Chinook, 33 coho, and three steelhead released for 431 boats (1,143 anglers): and no catch for six bank anglers.

Warrior Rock Lighthouse to Longview Bridge: Weekly checking showed 294 Chinook, 34 jack Chinook, and 14 coho kept, and 42 Chinook, seven jack Chinook, and six coho released for 234 boats (621 anglers); and no catch for 17 bank anglers.

Longview Bridge to West Puget Island: Weekly checking showed five Chinook kept for four boats (23 anglers).

West Puget Island to Tongue Point: Weekly checking showed four coho kept for one boat (two anglers).

Buoy 10: Weekly checking showed 199 Chinook and 1,464 coho kept, and 520 Chinook and 900 coho released for 1,442 boats (1,729 anglers).

Bonneville Pool: Weekly checking showed 140 Chinook, 23 jack Chinook, two coho, and one jack coho kept, and 44 Chinook and six jack Chinook released for 137 boats (401 anglers); and one Chinook kept for eight bank anglers.

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed 99 Chinook, 15 jack Chinook, and two coho kept, and nine Chinook, one jack Chinook, one coho, and one steelhead released for 149 boats (413 anglers); and three Chinook kept for nine bank anglers.

John Day Pool: Weekly checking showed no catch for nine boats (21 anglers).

STURGEON

Lower Columbia River: No report.

Bonneville Pool: No report.

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed 19 sublegal, 13 legal, and eight over-legal sized white sturgeon released for three boats (eight anglers); and two sublegal, 18 legal, and one over-legal sized white sturgeon released for three bank anglers.

John Day Pool: No report.

WALLEYE

Lower Columbia River (below Bonneville Dam): No report.

Bonneville Pool: Weekly checking showed 12 walleye kept for three boats (five anglers).

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed one walleye kept for three boats (eight anglers).

John Day Pool: Weekly checking showed 11 walleye kept, and seven walleye released for 18 boats (36 anglers).

SNAKE FISHING

September 10, 2026

Best bets for weekend fishing

  • Bass and trout can be caught downstream of Hells Canyon Dam.
  • Fall Chinook salmon reopened on August 18 on Snake River downstream of Hells Canyon Dam, harvest limits have been adjusted due to low return numbers. See the regulation updates page for more information.

Updates by section

BROWNLEE, OXBOW, AND HELLS CANYON RESERVOIRS: Trout, perch, crappie, bass, catfish, sturgeon

Fishing is good for warmwater species throughout the summer but can slow substantially midday as the summer warms and water temperatures increase. These reservoirs can form strong thermal layers with water devoid of Oxygen because of high nutrient loads. During the summer, harmful toxic algae blooms are common in these reservoirs, and swimming or letting pets in the water is not recommended.

When fishing in the summer, look for crappie suspending in open water or around structures. Try trolling small Rapalas on down riggers for crappie in the Powder River arm of Brownlee Reservoir. Some catfish and bass will be available in shallower water. For bass, expect a very light bite and be prepared to use some finesse to catch larger fish. However, once warm weather sets in, anglers may find the best success waiting until cool weather returns in the autumn after warm, oxygen depleted water conditions with toxic algae blooms have ended.

Brownlee Reservoir and Hells Canyon Reservoir are under advisories for harmful blue green algae, and the Powder Arm of Brownlee is currently under a precaution for harmful blue green algae. Follow this link to see the Oregon Health Authorities website showing harmful algae bloom advisories.

Reservoir levels can fluctuate greatly affecting which boat ramps are usable. Follow the links below to get up-to-date information on access along Brownlee Reservoir. Last updated 8/24/26.

Call the Idaho Power Company's recording at 1-800-422-3143 to get information on access at recreational sites or see the following link for Reservoir level information.

SNAKE RIVER below HELLS CANYON RESERVOIR: Trout, bass, sturgeon

Bass fishing can be phenomenal during the summer. Casting lures or soft plastic jigs toward rocks near shore is a very effective way of targeting bass in the Snake River. Most are smaller fish, but they are very numerous. Sturgeon fishing can be good in the Snake River downstream of Hells Canyon Dam. However, sturgeon fishing will be slower during the summer when water temperatures are warmer. All sturgeon must be released unharmed and cannot be removed from the water.

The Snake River downstream of Hells Canyon Dam will re-open for angling for fall Chinook salmon on August 18. However, due to low returns of Chinook salmon, harvest limits have been adjusted to only allow one wild (unclipped) Chinook salmon to be harvested per day. Please see the regulation updates page for more information.

Fishing for steelhead opened on September 1, however, most steelhead bound for Hells Canyon are still making their way up the Columbia and lower Snake Rivers. Steelhead fishing will probably be slow until more fish arrive later into October. Last updated 9/8/26.

Hells Canyon River flows can be found at this link.

SNAKE RIVER (above Brownlee Reservoir): Channel catfish, flathead catfish, smallmouth bass

This section of the Snake River above Brownlee Reservoir predominantly has catfish and bass that are well adapted to increased water temperatures. Although flows may decrease as water is used for crop irrigation, anglers can still find success fishing pools and back eddies where fish will congregate. Fishing near Farewell Bend State Park can be a productive area during the summer to target catfish from the bank and from boats. Because this section of river is free flowing, it is less susceptible to becoming Oxygen deprived or having toxic algae blooms. No new reports. Last updated 6/10/26.

There is a camera at Farewell Bend State Park to check the water level at the dock at this link.

MARINE FISHING

September 10, 2026

Announcements

Ocean salmon closed from Leadbetter Point, WA to Cape Falcon, OR:

  • Effective 11:59 PM Tuesday, September 8, 2026, the ocean recreational fishery in the area between Cape Falcon and Leadbetter Point (Columbia River Subarea) is closed to fishing for salmon. Possession of salmon on board a vessel is prohibited in the Columbia River Subarea.

Ocean coho salmon from Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain:

  • Effective Saturday, September 12, 2026, at 11:59PM, the recreational fishery from Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain is closed to the retention of coho salmon. The season remains open for all salmon except coho (Chinook salmon, 24" minimum length) with a daily bag limit of two salmon.

Report commercial derelict crab pots

If you are out on the ocean or in the Columbia River from now through the beginning of October, please report coordinates of any commercial derelict crab pots you see by emailing Jill.M.Smith@odfw.oregon.gov. These reports are distributed to derelict gear recovery permitted participants, enabling them to target gear recovery efforts now that the commercial crab season is closed in the ocean.

As of Jan. 1, 2026, an Ocean Endorsement is needed for most recreational anglers fishing in the ocean. Check the Ocean Endorsement page for more information.

Saltwater News Bulletins

Be among the first to know about in-season changes! You can subscribe to receive emails and text message alerts for marine topics that interest you. It's easy to unsubscribe at any time. Your contact information will remain confidential. Three different lists of interests to ocean enthusiasts are available: bottomfish, halibut and ocean salmon.

Albacore

It's that time of year when we are seeing albacore tuna off the Oregon coast! Anglers generally want to focus their effort on areas where the chlorophyll level is approximately 0.25mg. and sea surface temperatures are 58oF or higher. Chlorophyll and sea surface temperature data is available from the Oregon Coastal Ocean Observing System (OrCOOS).

Garibaldi: 1.35 albacore per angler

Pacific City: 0.33 albacore per angler

Depoe Bay: 2.85 albacore per angler

Newport: 4.58 albacore per angler

Charleston: 7 albacore per angler

Learn more about Tuna Fishing in Oregon.

Bottomfish

A few reminders

  • Visit the sport bottomfish seasons page to see what's new for 2026.
  • Retention of quillback rockfish and yelloweye rockfish remains prohibited.
  • Cabezon is prohibited from January 1 through June 30.

Port by port reports:

Garibaldi: Anglers landed 2.6 rockfish on average, mostly black, canary, and yellowtail rockfishes. Lingcod landings were slow at 0.25 fish per angler.

Depoe Bay: Mostly black rockfish were landed, with about 2.9 rockfish per angler. Lingcod catches were slow at 0.33 fish per angler.

Newport: Anglers landed 2.8 rockfish per person. Mostly black, deacon, canary and yellowtail rockfishes were observed. Lingcod was slow.

Charleston: Anglers landed around 3.3 rockfish, consisting of mainly black, canary, copper, yellowtail, and deacon rockfishes. Lingcod was slow at 0.33 fish per angler.

Brookings: Anglers caught just over 2.5 rockfish on average, mainly black, deacon, canary, and copper rockfishes. Lingcod was slow at 0.5 fish per angler.

The offshore long-leader fishery gives anglers an opportunity to catch more fish and to distribute effort away from nearshore species. Learn more about gear and the fishery.

Bottomfish fishing resources:

  • What can I keep and how many? Keep up with in-season regulation changes.
  • Know what you've caught with some helpful rockfish identification tips (including online quizzes and video).
  • Waypoints for fathom lines and other restricted areas.

Ocean salmon

Reminder: Ocean salmon anglers are reminded that they are limited to one rod, and no more than two single point, single shank, barbless hooks (no treble hooks) and that retention of jack salmon is not allowed in the ocean.

Ocean salmon fishing is closed in the recreational fishery in the area from Leadbetter Point, Washington to Cape Falcon, Oregon. Possession of salmon on board a vessel is prohibited in the Columbia River Subarea.

In the area from Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain, the non-mark selective coho season opened September 1 and will remain open through September 12, 2026 at 11:59PM. Open for all salmon, the daily bag limit is 2 salmon per day and both Chinook and coho can be either fin clipped or non-fin clipped. Effective Saturday, September 12, 2026, at 11:59PM, the recreational fishery from Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain is closed to the retention of coho salmon. The season remains open for all salmon except coho (Chinook salmon, 24" minimum length) with a daily bag limit of two salmon.

The area from Humbug Mountain to the Oregon/California border is closed to ocean salmon fishing beginning September 1 for the remainder of the year.

Shore and estuary fishing

Daily bag limits, seasons and licensing requirements for shore-based anglers are the same as for boat-based anglers.

There are plenty of rocky or sandy fishing sites up and down the coast where shore anglers can drop a line for saltwater fish. Read about how and where

Lingcod and many other bottomfish species are available year-round to shore anglers fishing in rocky areas. A common setup for lingcod is a jig head with a rubber swim bait – it's simple but effective. Also pack a measuring device for lingcod: the minimum legal size is 22 inches.

Surfperch are available in the surf year-round along sandy beaches and rocky shores, with the best fishing (and safest fishing) occurring when swells are small. Find surfperch and other learn to fish workshops and events here.

Want more opportunities that don't include a boat? Check out the crabbing and clamming recreation report for updates on crabs, clams, mussels and more!

When fishing from shore or inside estuaries and bays, it is important to check the tide. Many fish that swim into estuaries and bays, including salmon, surfperch, and Pacific herring, tend to come in with the tide. Catch of these species is more likely to occur closer to slack tide. Additionally, the accessibility of some areas can be completely dependent on the tide. Do not allow the incoming tide to become a safety issue.
